idiom_name: NestJS CanActivate guard (Reflector metadata) over a CASL ability
implementation_notes: In NestJS the enforcement point is a guard: a class implementing CanActivate, registered globally through APP_GUARD or per route with @UseGuards, returns false to produce 403 before the handler runs, and reads the required permissions from route metadata with Reflector + SetMetadata (the @Roles()/@RequirePermissions() decorator pattern in the official documentation). The decision belongs to a single ability object: CASL's AbilityBuilder/MongoAbility answers ability.can(action, subject) including attribute conditions such as authorId === user.id, and the guard consults it. The documentation warns that checking roles only at the handler level stops expressing per-operation permissions - the mapping belongs in the guard and the ability factory, not in services.
pitfalls: A guard applied per route is easy to forget on new endpoints; register it as APP_GUARD and let metadata opt out explicitly (deny when no metadata is present).
Returning true when the metadata is missing turns an unannotated route into an open one; the guard must deny by default.
Roles taken from a token are claims, not permissions: rebuild the ability server-side from the database so a stale or forged role cannot widen access.
